title: Towards Neuro-Symbolic Procedural Reasoning for Long-Horizon Vision-Language-Action Manipulation
abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models can execute short manipulation skills, but remain brittle in long-horizon procedures requiring persistent task state, dependency-aware reasoning, conditional decisions, and reliable grounding. We investigate a neuro-symbolic framework that combines learned VLA control with explicit task graphs and multimodal procedural memory. Task graphs encode action dependencies, valid transitions, and branch conditions, while memory maintains the active step, completed actions, textual context, and task-relevant visual evidence. Together, these structures guide object selection, destination grounding, subgoal dispatch, and verification of expected state transitions. Human demonstrations provide additional spatial and temporal guidance through gaze or saliency cues. To isolate their effect on policy learning, our initial study bypasses cross-view gaze transfer and directly annotates pseudo-gaze in robot-view teleoperation videos. The resulting guidance is used during VLA fine-tuning and inference. We study two long-horizon manipulation domains, workspace clearing and surgical-instrument handling, which require ordered execution, visually grounded decisions, and conditional branching. We evaluate correct-object and destination selection, subtask completion, task progress, step-order consistency, complete-task success, and procedural or execution mistakes. This work positions structured symbolic reasoning and demonstration-derived visual guidance as complementary mechanisms for reliable long-horizon VLA manipulation.

The resulting guidance is used during VLA fine-tuning and inference. We study two long-horizon manipulation domains, workspace clearing and surgical-instrument handling, which require ordered execution, visually grounded decisions, and conditional branching. We evaluate correct-object and destination selection, subtask completion, task progress, step-order consistency, complete-task success, and procedural or execution mistakes. This work positions structured symbolic reasoning and demonstration-derived visual guidance as complementary mechanisms for reliable long-horizon VLA manipulation.

title: Machine Unlearning as Private Retroactive Algorithms
abstract: Machine unlearning typically aims to emulate retraining from scratch: upon a deletion request, the unlearning algorithm should produce an outcome that would have been obtained had the deleted point never been included. Recent work has shown that this emulation requirement carries no meaningful privacy semantics against an adversary who observes a sequence of releases. Machine unlearning is thus not a privacy question per se, but rather a data maintenance question, which is precisely the subject of retroactive algorithms. These are algorithms supporting modifications of past operations, guaranteeing that all subsequent answers reflect the revised history as if it had always been in force. We put forward a definition of private retroactive algorithms, combining the retroactivity requirement with differential privacy under continual observation. We present constructions achieving both privacy and retroactivity at no asymptotic cost over privacy alone for linear statistics, clustering, and histograms, alongside impossibility results.

title: Constructing and Evaluating Clinical Reasoning Trajectories for Medical Agent
abstract: Evaluation of medical artificial intelligence agents remains predominantly answer-centric, assessing only the correctness of final outputs while overlooking the quality of intermediate reasoning. In clinical settings, however, a correct answer reached through fabricated evidence or incoherent logic is as dangerous as an incorrect one. We propose MedTraj, a framework that treats reasoning trajectories as critical objects for construction, evaluation, and optimization. The pipeline generates structured multi-step clinical reasoning chains from medical diagnosis sources. Each trajectory is then parsed into clinical observations, evidence, numbered reasoning steps, and a final conclusion, and scored across five quality dimensions: coherence, evidence support, hallucination, completeness, and traceability. Controlled error injection introduces targeted faults into otherwise correct trajectories to establish causal links between specific reasoning failures and measurable quality degradation. Building on this, step-level filtering based on marginal contribution identifies which individual reasoning steps drive or undermine trajectory quality. Finally, quality-weighted context learning feeds trajectory evaluations back into the model at inference time, allowing it to learn from both strong and weak reasoning demonstrations. Experiments across CareQA, PubMedQA, and CECMed demonstrate that trajectory context consistently improves reasoning coherence, with gains of +0.029 to +0.041 over a zero-shot baseline. On the CECMed severity assessment task, quality-weighted context nearly doubles the correctness over the zero-shot baseline while cutting the hallucination ratio by 87%. Marginal-contribution analysis further shows that a small minority (15.3%) of reasoning steps carry most of the quality signal, and that extending chains beyond four steps yields diminishing returns.

title: H2LooP Telecom Model v1: From Telecom Comprehension to Autonomous Issue and PR Resolution
abstract: We present H2LooP Telecom Model v1, a domain-specialized large language models fine-tuned for the telecommunications industry. We release two domain-adapted model variants serving complementary use cases: a comprehension-focused variant for telecom domain question answering and reasoning, and an agentic variant for autonomous telecom code generation, pull request resolution, and code commits on production repositories. H2LooP Telecom achieves strong results on the GSMA Open Telecom Lite (OT-Lite) benchmark and a proprietary telecom code generation benchmark, outperforming frontier closed-source models such as GPT-5 and Claude Opus on independent leaderboard evaluation, while preserving general-purpose capabilities. The Comprehension variant achieves 81.8% weighted average on OT-Lite Pass@3, and, independently, ranks 5th overall on the official community-run Open Telco AI Leaderboard* at only 31B parameters-ahead of frontier closed-source systems including Claude Opus 4.6, GPT-5, Gemini 3 Flash, Grok-4-fast, and Kimi K2.5. Our agentic variant obtains a relative improvement of +8.8% in AST Similarity and +20.0% in Location IoU over the base model on telecom code generation, while maintaining identical MMLU (74.0%) and BFCL v3 multi-turn function calling (79.0%) performance, indicating zero catastrophic forgetting. Domain specialization on curated telecom corpora, spanning 3GPP standards, O-RAN specifications, network telemetry, and real repository commits, yields substantial improvements over general-purpose models of equivalent scale, approaches frontier closed-source models on domain-specific evaluation, and is independently corroborated by our official leaderboard standing.

title: From Attested GPU Computation to Authorized Action: Execution Finality for AI Accelerators and Confidential Workloads
abstract: Remote attestation can establish important properties of CPUs, confidential virtual machines, GPUs, AI accelerators, DPUs, SmartNICs, firmware and workload environments. However, successful appraisal of a computational environment does not, without an operation-specific authorization decision, determine whether each consequential operation generated by that environment should become externally effective. This work presents an attestation-bound execution-finality architecture for AI accelerators and confidential workloads. A consequence-bearing operation—such as an API invocation, infrastructure change, storage mutation, payment instruction or cross-workload request—is first represented as a canonical Candidate Act in a Non-Effective State. An Execution-Finality Validator evaluates that act using applicable Attestation Results, workload identity, authorization scope, target identity, policy, freshness and transaction context. Successful validation produces signed, narrowly scoped execution authority cryptographically bound to the security-relevant content of the Candidate Act. At the Finality Sink—the boundary where the proposed operation would first acquire external effect—the system reconstructs the actual operation and verifies its signature, act digest, audience, transaction identity, freshness and replay state before permitting effectuation. A runnable, vendor-neutral reference implementation accompanies the architecture. It implements deterministic CBOR encoding, COSE_Sign1 signatures using Ed25519, signed EAT issuance and appraisal, act-bound Execution Handles, an enforcing API gateway, atomic replay protection, deterministic cryptographic test vectors and adversarial tests. The implementation demonstrates rejection of missing authority, modified amounts, substituted destinations, changed paths, incorrect audiences, expired handles, altered signatures, unacceptable attestation measurements and repeated presentation of previously consumed authority. Eleven automated tests, including an end-to-end HTTP validation and gateway-enforcement flow, pass successfully. Local microbenchmarks measured approximately 140 microseconds median for EAT appraisal, 1.5 microseconds for Candidate Act construction, 50 microseconds for Execution Handle issuance and approximately 140 microseconds for handle verification. These results characterize the portable reference implementation only and are not claims about GPU, DPU, SmartNIC or hyperscale production performance. The architecture complements—not replaces—the IETF RATS architecture, Entity Attestation Tokens, COSE, workload identity, confidential computing and existing authorization systems. Its proposed contribution is end-to-end correspondence between the operation evaluated by the authorization function and the operation accepted at the protected effectuation boundary. The software is a working reference implementation and interoperability demonstrator, not a production-certified accelerator, cloud or payment system. Hardware-integrated deployment requires platform-specific trust anchors, protected key management, non-bypassable effectuation paths, distributed replay state and independent security review.

title: Title: Quantum Entanglement Propagation via Phase-Space Synchronization
abstract: Quantum entanglement, a cornerstone of quantum information processing, remains a formidable hurdle in achieving robust and reliable communication. Decoherence, a primary source of this challenge, limits the range and stability of entanglement. This paper explores a novel algorithm for propagating quantum entanglement across macroscopic distances by synchronizing the evolution of entangled states within phase-space representations. We propose a dynamic phase-space mapping technique that allows for precise tracking and manipulation of entanglement fidelity, addressing a fundamental challenge in quantum communication and teleportation – the issue of entanglement decoherence. The algorithm leverages a continuously evolving phase space, enabling the precise control of entangled states and mitigating the effects of environmental noise. This research contributes to a significant advancement in the field of quantum entanglement propagation, offering a viable pathway towards practical quantum communication and teleportation.

title: Title: Adaptive Quantum Algorithm for Non-Linear Optimization
abstract: This paper introduces an innovative adaptive quantum algorithm designed to address the limitations of traditional optimization techniques, particularly when dealing with non-linear problems. The algorithm leverages reinforcement learning to dynamically adjust its parameters based on the input data, offering a significant improvement over static optimization methods. We present a detailed architecture, including the core mechanism and initial implementation, demonstrating its effectiveness in a range of non-linear optimization scenarios. The goal is to provide a robust and efficient solution for complex optimization challenges across diverse fields.

title: Adaptive Topology Matrix Computation
abstract: This paper presents a novel self-adaptive topology matrix computation framework leveraging quantum entanglement for efficient computation and automatic parameter adjustment. Traditional approaches to topology matrix calculations suffer from computational limitations, prompting a need for innovative methods. This work introduces a dynamic algorithm that exploits the unique properties of quantum entanglement to optimize the computation of topological matrices. The core mechanism centers around dynamically adjusting the matrix's features based on the entangled state, enabling significantly enhanced computational efficiency. This research addresses the limitations of conventional methods and offers a promising avenue for future developments in topological matrix analysis. The paper details the framework's architecture, the underlying entanglement-based optimization process, and its practical implementation with illustrative examples. The investigation explores the potential of this approach to tackle complex topological matrix problems, offering a new perspective on their computational feasibility.

title: Fractal-Based Self-Organizing Algorithms for Quantum Control
abstract: This paper explores the application of fractal-based self-organizing algorithms to quantum control. Quantum systems, due to their inherent sensitivity to initial conditions, often suffer from instability and require sophisticated control strategies. Traditional control methods can be brittle, leading to oscillations and inaccuracies. We propose a novel approach utilizing fractal geometry to generate self-consistent, predictable patterns within quantum systems. This design aims to enhance precision, stability, and the overall controllability of quantum states. The core mechanism involves creating a fractal-shaped structure that guides the quantum system, promoting a more stable and responsive response to external perturbations. This paper details the design of these algorithms, presents preliminary results demonstrating their effectiveness, and discusses the potential implications for advanced quantum technologies.

title: Quantum-Inspired Topology for Optimization – Adaptive Representation
abstract: This paper explores the application of quantum-inspired topology to optimization, specifically focusing on the development of a novel method for representing and manipulating complex landscape structures. The core claim is that by leveraging non-linear relationships and entanglement principles, we can create a topology that guides the search process more effectively, leading to improved solution quality. The proposed framework introduces a dynamically adjusted representation of the search space, enabling adaptive exploration and mitigating the limitations of traditional optimization techniques. We detail the mathematical foundation of this approach, including the key topological invariants and their impact on the search dynamics. The paper will discuss the advantages of this methodology, including increased efficiency, improved exploration of the search space, and the potential for discovering novel solutions.

title: Quantum Entanglement Non-Locality Modeling and Control
abstract: Quantum entanglement, a fundamental phenomenon in quantum mechanics, exhibits properties that challenge classical physics' notions of locality. This research investigates the potential of leveraging entanglement for non-local control, aiming to overcome the limitations imposed by traditional quantum computation. We propose a novel model based on a dynamically evolving quantum state graph, utilizing the non-locality inherent in entangled states to guide a control algorithm. This algorithm incorporates adaptive mechanisms to precisely manipulate the entangled state, thereby opening avenues for exploring and harnessing non-local quantum operations. The study addresses the current limitations in entanglement-based quantum control, offering a potential pathway toward more versatile and powerful quantum systems.

title: Emergent Information Encoding via Fractal Topology
abstract: This paper introduces a novel method for information encoding and retrieval leveraging fractal topology. We propose a 'Fractal Semantic Map' – a dynamically evolving structure composed of self-similar fractal elements that encodes data through interconnectedness and self-similarity. The resulting map enables efficient searching and retrieval, surpassing traditional data representation techniques in terms of compression and scalability. We detail the core mechanism, including the construction of the fractal map and the associated algorithms for encoding and accessing information. The potential benefits of this approach are significant for data compression, search, and pattern recognition.

title: Quantum States and Non-Linear Mapping: A New Approach to High-Dimensional Geometry
abstract: Quantum states, characterized by superposition and entanglement, represent a fundamental aspect of quantum mechanics. This research explores the application of non-linear mapping techniques to quantum states, aiming to leverage these properties for the construction of advanced geometric models and optimization algorithms. The core claim is that the ability to map quantum states to high-dimensional geometric spaces can significantly simplify geometric modeling, improve computational efficiency, and unlock new possibilities in geometric analysis. This work focuses on demonstrating the potential of this approach through a rigorous theoretical investigation and preliminary experimental exploration using simplified geometric constructs.

title: Quantum State Resonance Control and Modulation
abstract: Quantum state resonance control and modulation is a burgeoning field within quantum information science, offering unprecedented opportunities for manipulating and encoding quantum information. This paper explores the application of quantum state resonance control to achieve highly efficient quantum state manipulation. We propose a novel algorithm based on the non-linear properties of quantum states, specifically designed to precisely control the resonant frequencies and amplitudes of quantum systems. The core of this approach involves a self-adaptive resonance mechanism, allowing for dynamic optimization of the quantum state. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this method through simulations and preliminary experimental validation, revealing the potential for significant advancements in quantum information processing and encoding. The proposed approach represents a fundamental shift in how we approach quantum control, paving the way for new quantum information modalities.

We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through a series of numerical experiments on several prominent topological information processing tasks, showcasing substantial speedups compared to existing methods. This work represents a significant advancement in the field, offering a pathway toward more efficient and scalable topological information algorithms.

title: Quantum Entanglement-Driven Distributed Computation Verification
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to distributed computation verification leveraging the unique properties of quantum entanglement. The core idea is to establish a highly reliable verification chain between distributed computation nodes utilizing entanglement, effectively detecting and correcting errors that may arise during computation. Traditional distributed computation verification methods rely heavily on classical communication and data redundancy, often struggling with scalability and security. Our approach, however, utilizes entangled states to enable real-time state synchronization and error detection without requiring classical communication. This fundamentally changes the verification process, offering inherent resilience against errors even when individual nodes fail. The system relies on encoding computational results into quantum states and exploiting the correlations inherent in entangled states to identify and rectify discrepancies. The theoretical framework presented here demonstrates the potential for surpassing the limitations of classical computation in terms of fault tolerance and security. Key mathematical concepts including quantum state representation, entanglement quantification, and error detection protocols are outlined. The proposed method provides a pathway towards building robust and secure distributed computing systems suitable for demanding applications such as secure multi-party computation and large-scale scientific simulations. ---

title: 基于动态拓扑图的认知架构自适应优化
abstract: This paper proposes a novel cognitive architecture based on a dynamically adapting topology, termed a Neuro-Topological Network (NTN). The core claim is that cognitive architecture performance can be significantly improved by dynamically adjusting its internal topology to better accommodate evolving task demands and environmental changes, leading to more efficient cognitive processes. The NTN utilizes a reinforcement learning (RL) approach to optimize its topology in real-time. Nodes within the NTN represent cognitive modules (e.g., memory, reasoning, attention), while connection weights represent the interaction strength between these modules. The architecture adapts based on factors such as task difficulty, input complexity, and internal system activity. The optimization goals are to minimize task completion time, error rate, and resource consumption. The optimization strategies involve dynamic node addition/removal, weight adjustment, and routing strategy modifications. This approach contrasts with traditional static cognitive architectures and offers a more flexible and adaptive solution for complex cognitive tasks. The key contribution lies in applying reinforcement learning to the entire architecture topology, promoting holistic and efficient cognitive processes.

title: Quantum-Enhanced Simulation of Material Phase Transitions – Modeling Emergent Phenomena with Quantum Accuracy
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to simulating material phase transitions, leveraging the power of quantum mechanics to achieve unprecedented accuracy in modeling emergent phenomena. Traditional methods often struggle with the complex correlations inherent in these transitions, leading to inaccuracies and limitations in understanding the underlying physics. We introduce a quantum-enhanced simulation framework centered around quantum algorithms designed to accurately capture these subtle correlations, offering a significant advancement in the modeling of superconductivity, magnetism, and other complex phase transitions. The core mechanism involves simulating the evolution of the material's quantum state using quantum algorithms, while simultaneously incorporating a sophisticated correlation model to address the inherent difficulties of classical simulations. This paper details the design of the quantum simulation framework, explores its theoretical advantages, and presents preliminary results demonstrating its efficacy in simulating key phase transition scenarios.

title: Probability Logic Quantum Computing (PLQC)
abstract: Probability Logic Quantum Computing (PLQC) presents a novel approach to quantum computing by integrating the fundamental principles of probability logic into the core computational process. This research explores the potential of leveraging the inherent strengths of probability logic – such as its ability to handle uncertainty and probabilistic outcomes – to enhance the efficiency and stability of quantum algorithms. The core mechanism focuses on modifying quantum gate operations and quantum circuit design to actively incorporate probabilistic elements, thereby mitigating the inherent challenges of quantum systems. This paper investigates the feasibility of implementing PLQC, outlining its potential benefits and challenges, and providing a preliminary analysis of its design principles. The goal is to establish a robust and scalable framework for quantum computing that surpasses the limitations of traditional approaches.

title: Title: Non-Markovian Quantum State Collapse for Quantum Simulation
abstract: Quantum state collapse is a fundamental process in quantum mechanics, crucial for generating observable outcomes from initial quantum states. Current simulation methods often rely on approximations that limit the fidelity of quantum simulations, particularly for complex systems. This paper investigates a novel framework for quantum state collapse that explicitly incorporates non-Markovian dynamics, aiming to improve the accuracy and computational efficiency of quantum simulations. We propose a new algorithm based on analyzing the system's dynamics and dynamically adjusting collapse parameters to enhance the fidelity of the simulation. The core claim is that this approach offers a significant advancement in quantum simulation, enabling more accurate modeling of complex quantum systems by addressing limitations of current methods. This work focuses on developing a robust and adaptable methodology to handle non-Markovian systems, ultimately providing a pathway towards more reliable quantum simulations.

title: 基于多尺度自适应的非线性数据聚类
abstract: This paper introduces a novel data clustering technique, termed "Adaptive Multi-Scale Data Clustering" (AMDC), that leverages the inherent variability of data across multiple scales to achieve accurate and effective clustering. Traditional clustering methods often struggle with data distributions that deviate significantly across different scales. AMDC employs a dynamic adjustment of cluster boundaries based on the data's characteristics, allowing for a more robust and adaptable clustering process. This approach significantly enhances data quality and reveals underlying patterns within datasets with varying levels of complexity. The core mechanism of AMDC is based on iteratively refining cluster boundaries using a multi-scale density estimation scheme, incorporating a novel adaptive weighting factor to prioritize data points that influence cluster structure. The results demonstrate that AMDC outperforms existing methods on a diverse range of benchmark datasets, showcasing its potential for applications across various domains.

title: 基于图的非线性自适应数据压缩
abstract: This paper presents a novel data compression algorithm based on graph structure, designed to handle non-linear data distributions and automatically adapt to changes in data patterns. Traditional data compression techniques often focus solely on the data itself, failing to leverage the inherent structure of the data to achieve optimal compression. Our approach utilizes a graph representation to model data, employing a dynamically adaptive compression strategy to minimize redundancy. We demonstrate the algorithm's effectiveness through rigorous analysis, focusing on improved compression ratios and robustness to data variations. The core mechanism involves constructing a graph representation, applying a self-adaptive compression technique, and evaluating the resulting compression performance. The paper concludes with a discussion of the algorithm's strengths and potential applications in various data storage and transmission scenarios.

title: Design Docs Are All You Need: An AI-native Machine-Learning Performance Tool
abstract: Machine-learning performance modeling is a uniquely hostile terrain for long-lived software: the assumptions baked into today's abstractions are invalidated by tomorrow's models and systems, forcing perpetual refactoring of performance-modeling frameworks. Meanwhile, AI coding agents have become fast and capable enough that regenerating an entire library is cheaper than paying down the tech debt of incrementally patching it. We describe SMART, a rigorous symbolic performance-modeling library for ML systems whose main branch contains almost no code: the repository is a DAG of self-contained natural-language design docs, coding sub-agents regenerate the implementation from only the docs on new version updates, and every human change is a natural-language edit to a doc--self-documenting by construction. Two ingredients make regeneration reliable: (i) a design-doc style built around step-by-step worked examples that act as in-context demonstrations for the generating agents, and (ii) a minimal, recursively defined operator IR with symbolic (SymPy) cost expressions, a fast analytical roll-up mode for large sweeps, and a slow modulo-scheduling mode for fine-grained schedule studies. Regenerated implementations reproduce hand-audited reference models--including DeepSeek-V3 serving on a TPU pod slice--to round-off precision, suggesting that design docs--not code--can be the durable artifact for ML-systems co-design tools.

title: Measuring AI Accountability Through Argumentation Analysis: Can Model Reasoning Withstand Scrutiny?
abstract: AI oversight methods rely on ground truth for validation, but what constitutes appropriate AI behavior is contested. This leaves evaluation of moral reasoning in LLMs and debate-based oversight implicitly avoiding realistic ambiguity. We investigate an alternative standard designed to function despite such ambiguity: structural quality of the defence a model can mount for its verdicts in response to critical questions, measured through a four-phase dialectical protocol grounded in Walton's theory of argumentation schemes and Govier's criteria for argument cogency. The protocol is adaptive to different frames of reasoning, extends beyond multiple-choice framing, and treats both the reasoning that precedes a verdict and its post-hoc justification. Across nine frontier models and 200 high-ambiguity MoralChoice items -- $6,778$ judge-scored cells, validated against $89.6\%$ inter-judge agreement on the binary failure judgment -- models defend their reasoning well above the rubric minimum on every dimension. Failure mass concentrates on grounds and sufficiency, and correlates with epistemic hedging rather than argument length. Reasoning is better defended than post-hoc justification, on every model and every Govier dimension. The scheme a model presents in its justification differs from the one it reasoned with on a substantial share of dilemmas ($\geq 20\%$ per model), despite value-based practical reasoning dominating both tracks. The protocol catches strictly indefensible defences (self-contradiction, false premises), and it surfaces difficulties in characterizing the role of retraction in AI alignment, suggesting a need for more situated evaluations.

title: Dual-Part Multi-Lateral Branched Network for Multi-Class Segmentation in Cardiovascular Catheterization Angiograms
abstract: Catheterisation image processing requires segmentation models that are fast, accurate and explainable. While most of the existing studies usually focus on binary segmentation, there is a recent demand for simultaneous segmentation of multiple structures found in catheterization scenes. In this study, a dual-part MLBNet architecture is designed with multi-lateral encoder blocks and multi-head decoder branches for class-aware segmentation in cardiovascular catheterization scenes. Lateral branches in the encoder enables repeated feature extraction to learn diverse shared representations, while multiple decoder heads are used to introduce class-skewed branches that specialize in different structural properties in catheterization scenes. To analyze the performances of the dual-part MLBNet architecture, several multi-class segmentation angiogram data obtained during cardiovascular catheterization in phantom models, synthetic human-simulated aorta, and animal model are used for model training and evaluation. Results obtained showed the dual-part models could effectively separate guidewire, catheter, vessels and background pixels to their classes of memberships with high probability. The results demonstrate that all models were able to distinguish the dominant background class from foreground structures with high overall accuracy.

title: Newton Matching for Generative Modeling: A Unified Framework for Fine-Tuning and Sampling
abstract: We develop Newton Matching, a unified framework for fine-tuning and sampling in generative modeling. The target is $π\proptoμe^{τr}$, where $r$ is the reward, $τ>0$ the inverse temperature, and $μ$ denotes the pretrained model's terminal density for fine-tuning or the constant $1$ for sampling. We shift the paradigm from isolated losses to iterative optimization over canonical models: population minimizers of standard conditional matching for terminal densities. Under compatible smooth-realization assumptions, canonical velocities form a manifold diffeomorphic to the density manifold. Transporting the Fisher-Rao metric and mixture connection to this manifold, we show that the reverse-KL Hessian equals the metric, so the Newton direction coincides with the negative Fisher-Rao gradient. At terminal density $ρ$, each stage takes a tangential step generated by the regularized reward $r-\frac1τ\log(ρ/μ)$, followed by terminal-density-preserving canonicalization. This canonical retraction yields an exact finite-stepsize density characterization. For the ideal iteration, we prove strict reverse-KL descent away from the target for $0 < η\le τ$, global convergence under mild conditions, and local quadratic convergence for full steps ($η=τ$). Covariance and gradient forms, each with forward or reverse regression-pair constructions, yield sample-wise tangential-update losses with the same population minimizer, without importance sampling or full-trajectory backpropagation. We develop approximate updates and define critical-point consistency as vanishing tangential displacement if and only if $ρ=π$. We recover representative methods as exact realizations, critical-point-consistent approximations, or objective-altering variants, enabling modular algorithm design. Our work advances the theory and algorithms of reinforcement learning for generative models.

title: PAC-Bayesian Reconstruction Guarantees for Time Series Variational Autoencoders
abstract: Forecasting time series accurately is critical for applications with complex data ranging from energy systems to healthcare and finance. Among current state of the art models, generative latent variable models are increasingly implemented; yet principled generalisation guarantees for modern latent variable models remain limited. In particular, while Variational AutoEncoders are widely used for sequential data, their theoretical analysis is largely restricted to i.i.d. settings. In this work, we develop a PAC-Bayesian framework for latent variables models applied to time series. Building on reconstruction-based bounds, we extend PAC-Bayesian guarantees to Markovian latent structures, capturing temporal dependencies through a sequential generative process. These guarantees do not grow with the length of the trajectory. Our bounds depend on assumptions which are common in the literature; we provide an example framework where they would be verified to show that they are not as restrictive as they may seem.

title: Beyond Stationarity in Time Series: Discovering Causal Structures and Latent Regimes via Markov Blankets
abstract: This paper introduces Regime-aware Constraint-Based and Noise-Based causal discovery with Markov Blankets (RCBNB-MB), a novel causal discovery algorithm for time series that relaxes the common assumption of a single, time-consistent causal structure. Time series are typically observed at discrete time points and often exhibit regime changes that challenge the assumption of a static causal structure, a limitation in many real-world dynamic systems. To address this challenge, RCBNB-MB identifies latent causal regimes, defined as subsets of time points within which a stable causal structure holds. The algorithm follows an iterative strategy that segments the time series into regimes and discovers the causal graph within each regime. By leveraging the Markov blanket rather than direct parents, RCBNB-MB gains robustness to errors in causal discovery and preserves predictive information. We provide theoretical guarantees for RCBNB-MB's ability to recover both regime transitions and causal graphs under reasonable assumptions. Furthermore, we validate its effectiveness through extensive experiments on simulated datasets with known ground truth and real-world IT monitoring data, where taking into account regime shifts is critical. Empirical results show that RCBNB-MB systematically outperforms baseline approaches in accurately detecting regime changes and their associated causal graphs, positioning it as a robust and versatile framework for non-stationary time series analysis.

title: Conformal Prediction for Offensive Security
abstract: Despite its introduction more than a quarter century ago, Conformal Prediction (CP) has seen surprisingly few applications to the cyber security world thus far. In particular, we observe that, while CP has been employed as a defensive measure in many recent works, its use for carrying out attacks (i.e., for offensive security) is hard to trace in the literature. We explore this gap, by presenting initial findings in two key areas of offensive security: Privacy-Preserving Machine Learning, and network traffic analysis.

title: Intra-Prompt Parallel Decoding for Common-Context Question Answering
abstract: In common-context question answering (CCQA) tasks, multiple input questions share a common context to base their answers from. However, Large Language Models typically generate each answer using an independent prompt. While existing batching and caching techniques help improve parallelism and reduce repeated computations, the separation of questions across prompts limits the achievable speedup, as modern GPUs are underutilized due to a memory bottleneck during attention. We present Intra-Prompt Parallel Decoding (IPPD), a novel inference method that answers multiple common-context questions in parallel within a single prompt. IPPD directly addresses the bottleneck by efficiently sharing both memory and computation during the attention process, as the next token for every question is decoded in a single inference step. IPPD uses virtual position IDs and attention mask manipulation to generate the same output as standard prompting without requiring fine-tuning or any changes to the LLM architecture. Since all parallelism occurs within a prompt, IPPD is fully compatible with batched inference, even when each prompt features a different context. Our experiments show that IPPD delivers up to 7X the effective throughput as standard decoding without quality degradation, and outperforms prefix caching with PagedAttention in most settings.

title: FedDRAW: Federated Dual Reputation Annealing Weighting for Heterogeneous Multi-Institutional Chest Radiograph Classification
abstract: Artificial intelligence models are promising for medical diagnosis, but they require large numbers of unbiased data, which in medicine are distributed across hospitals and cannot be centralized to protect patient privacy. Federated Learning (FL) addresses this, since hospitals train one shared diagnostic model while patient data remain local. Training proceeds in communication rounds, in which each hospital trains the shared model locally and returns it to the server for merging by weighted average. This aggregation weight determines whose institutional knowledge shapes the result. Federated averaging (FedAvg) sets it in proportion to local sample count, so a small but informative hospital is permanently assigned a small influence, andl argest clients could dominate the global model even when they are less informative. We propose Federated Dual Reputation Annealing Weighting (FedDRAW), a server-side aggregation method that combines a data-size prior with the cosine similarity between client and global parameters under two coupled annealing schedules. An inner schedule shifts client reputation from the size prior towards similarity. An outer, deferred annealing schedule on the softmax inverse temperature keeps the weighting selective in the early and middle rounds and relaxes it to uniformity at convergence. We evaluate FedDRAW on 12 simulated client-partition scenarios of two chest radiograph datasets (CheXpert and ChestMNIST), against seven federated baselines under identical local training settings. FedDRAW achieved the highest average rank among all eight methods under both AUC and the geometric mean (GM) of sensitivity and specificity, which a Friedman test with Nemenyi post-hoc analysis confirmed to be a statistically significant difference between the methods. Scheduling two signals, rather than fixing the weights by sample count alone, could enable less biased diagnostic models.

title: 基于量子纠缠的拓扑结构分析
abstract: This paper investigates the potential of quantum entanglement to revolutionize the field of topological structure analysis. Traditional methods often rely on handcrafted parameters and are computationally expensive. We propose a novel quantum algorithm leveraging entangled states to efficiently identify and analyze complex topological structures. The core mechanism centers around dynamically adjusting the entanglement parameters to probe the structure's inherent properties. The paper details the algorithm's design, its potential advantages over existing techniques, and a preliminary exploration of its application to specific topological phenomena. The investigation highlights the promise of quantum entanglement as a powerful tool for uncovering intricate topological landscapes.

title: Dynamic Geometric Constraint Optimization for Probabilistic Model Enhancement
abstract: This paper introduces a novel dynamic geometric constraint optimization approach for probabilistic model enhancement. Traditional methods often rely on manual parameter adjustment, limiting the model's flexibility and potential for optimization. We propose a framework where the probability model itself is treated as a geometric structure, allowing for an automatic optimization process guided by geometric constraints and probabilistic distributions. This method leverages the interplay between these factors to improve model prediction accuracy. We detail the core mechanism, including the geometric representation of the model, the optimization process, and the resulting improvements in predictive performance. The paper demonstrates the effectiveness of this approach through a series of numerical experiments, showcasing significant gains in accuracy compared to traditional methods.

title: Information Theory Quantum Key Distribution Protocol Optimization
abstract: Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) promises unconditionally secure communication based on the laws of physics. This paper explores the application of information theory to optimize the key distribution process within a QKD protocol. We propose an algorithm that leverages quantum entanglement to enhance key distribution efficiency and security. The core mechanism involves manipulating the state of entangled particles to shift the key towards a more secure state. The paper presents a novel approach to optimize the entanglement parameters, demonstrating potential improvements in key generation and security compared to existing QKD protocols. The study analyzes the impact of optimized entanglement on key generation, focusing on the reduction of computational complexity and the amplification of the security level.

title: Quantum State Mapping and High-Dimensional Geometry-Adaptive Algorithms
abstract: Quantum state mapping represents a paradigm shift in computational geometry, offering the potential to model complex geometric structures with unprecedented precision and efficiency. This paper investigates the application of non-linear mapping techniques to quantum states, exploring their utility in high-dimensional geometric modeling and optimization. We demonstrate how these mappings can generate more robust geometric representations and significantly enhance computational performance. The core mechanism centers around the creation of a mapping that transforms a high-dimensional quantum state into a lower-dimensional geometric space, simplifying geometric analysis and enabling novel optimization strategies. This research proposes a new algorithmic framework that leverages non-linear mappings to construct increasingly sophisticated geometric models, ultimately pushing the boundaries of geometric computation.

title: Quantum Entanglement-Based Multi-Layered Space Optimization for Information Encoding and Decoding
abstract: This paper investigates a novel approach to quantum information encoding and decoding utilizing multi-layered entangled states. The core claim is that strategically employing these states significantly enhances the efficiency and security of information processing. The proposed mechanism leverages meticulously designed multi-layer entangled state topologies, capitalizing on the unique properties of quantum entanglement to facilitate superposition encoding and parallel decoding across multiple paths. This approach inherently minimizes the risk of information leakage. We explore the theoretical underpinnings of this method, focusing on the mathematical framework and the optimization strategies involved. The key contributions lie in the development of a framework for designing multi-layered entangled states specifically tailored for information transmission, and a corresponding decoding protocol that exploits the correlated nature of these states. We present a mathematical model outlining the information transfer process and discuss the potential for scaling this approach to larger information capacities. The final section details the optimization criteria and potential future research directions.

The core mechanism lies in the introduction of a dynamic topology, which allows for the continuous and adaptive modification of feature representations, leading to improved model generalization and adaptability. title: Self-Correcting Neural Networks using Recurrent Error Correction
abstract: Traditional neural networks often struggle with error accumulation during training, resulting in reduced accuracy and instability. This paper proposes a novel architecture for neural networks, termed Self-Correcting Neural Networks (SCNNs), which leverages recurrent connections and an integrated error correction module. The core mechanism involves a recurrent neural network structure where an error correction component continuously monitors the network's internal representations and applies corrections to mitigate error propagation. This approach aims to enhance the network's stability, improve its convergence speed, and ultimately achieve superior performance compared to conventional training methods. The system is designed to dynamically adjust its internal state based on detected errors, fostering a more robust and accurate learning process. This work presents a theoretical framework and a conceptual design for SCNNs, highlighting their potential to address the limitations of existing neural network training techniques.

abstract: Quantum entanglement, a fundamental phenomenon in quantum mechanics, holds immense potential for revolutionizing computation. However, realizing this potential requires sophisticated optimization techniques, particularly when dealing with complex entangled states. This paper explores the application of parameterized adaptive algorithms to optimize quantum computation, focusing on the unique properties of non-symmetric entanglement. We introduce a novel approach that leverages the inherent asymmetry of entangled states to achieve performance enhancements, particularly in systems exhibiting complex non-symmetry. The core mechanism involves dynamically adjusting parameters to steer the entangled state towards optimal configurations. This research demonstrates the effectiveness of this approach through theoretical analysis and preliminary experimentation on specific quantum systems, suggesting a significant advancement over existing optimization methods.

title: Distributed Computation via Quantum Phase Slip
abstract: This paper proposes a novel distributed computation protocol leveraging the subtle properties of quantum phase slip induced by decoherence. The core idea is to utilize controlled phase slips to facilitate efficient information exchange and computation among multiple quantum nodes without requiring complex entanglement distribution. We detail a protocol where the rate and direction of phase slips are precisely manipulated, allowing for correlated quantum states to emerge and perform computations. The protocol's efficiency stems from minimizing the need for pre-shared entanglement, a significant bottleneck in existing distributed quantum computation approaches. We present a mathematical formulation of the protocol, focusing on the key parameters governing phase slip dynamics and their impact on computational outcomes. The proposed method offers a promising avenue for scalable distributed quantum computation, particularly in scenarios where resource-constrained quantum networks are employed. This work highlights a new paradigm for quantum computation by harnessing inherent quantum noise.

title: Explainable AI for Cybersecurity Threat Detection – Causal Reasoning from Log Data
abstract: Cybersecurity threat detection systems are increasingly reliant on Artificial Intelligence (AI) models, but these systems frequently operate as "black boxes," making it difficult for human analysts to understand *why* a particular activity is flagged as a threat. This paper proposes a novel Explainable AI (XAI) system designed to address this challenge by leveraging causal reasoning techniques applied to log data. The system learns and represents causal relationships between log events and identified cybersecurity threats. This allows for the generation of human-understandable explanations for threat detections, providing analysts with valuable insights into the root causes of suspicious activity. The core contribution of this work lies in moving beyond opaque AI models and offering a transparent, interpretable framework for cybersecurity threat analysis. The system's architecture incorporates probabilistic graphical models to represent these causal relationships, enabling inference and explanation generation. Evaluation metrics focus on the accuracy and comprehensibility of the generated explanations, demonstrating the potential of causal reasoning to enhance trust and effectiveness in cybersecurity threat detection.

This approach offers a promising avenue for enhancing the performance of quantum algorithms in complex scenarios. The paper explores the potential benefits of this dynamic topology approach, including improved convergence rates, enhanced solution space exploration, and adaptability to varying problem characteristics. We present a preliminary implementation demonstrating the efficacy of this method on a simplified quantum optimization problem.

title: Моделирование офлайн-последовательного принятия решений для мета-оптимизации чёрного ящика на основе усиленного консервативного Q-обучения
abstract: Объект: процесс управления гиперпараметрами дифференциальной эволюции в задачах оптимизации чёрного ящика. Предмет: методы и алгоритмы офлайн-обучения с подкреплением на основе моделей пространства состояний для адаптивного управления параметрами эволюционных алгоритмов. Методы и методология проведения ВКР: методы дифференциальной эволюции; офлайн-обучение с подкреплением; консервативное Q-обучение (CQL); модели пространства состояний (Mamba); метод Монте-Карло Dropout; двухбазисное экспоненциальное скользящее среднее (EMA); бенчмаркинг BBOB; язык Python, PyTorch. В связи с высокой вычислительной стоимостью целевой функции и отсутствием аналитического дифференцирования в задачах оптимизации чёрного ящика в настоящей работе предлагается фреймворк адаптивного управления гиперпараметрами Q‑Mamba, основанный на моделях пространства состояний и офлайн-обучении с подкреплением. В рамках фреймворка задача управления гиперпараметрами дифференциальной эволюции формулируется как задача офлайн-метаобучения с подкреплением: в качестве магистральной сети используется селективная модель пространства состояний Mamba, обеспечивающая моделирование зависимостей в длинных оптимизационных траекториях с линейной вычислительной сложностью. Для решения характерных для офлайн-обучения проблем смещения распределения и завышения оценок Q-функции разработан алгоритм адаптивного консервативного Q-обучения Adaptive CQL с двухбазисной экспоненциальной скользящей средней. В алгоритме задействована оценка неопределённости методом Монте-Карло Dropout, что позволяет динамически регулировать коэффициент консервативной регуляризации λ, реализуя принцип «разумной осторожности»: поддержание высокой консервативности в областях с разреженными данными и ослабление ограничений в областях с высокой плотностью данных для усиления исследовательской способности стратегии. Эксперименты на эталонных функциях BBOB и синтетических задачах нейроэволюции показали, что по сравнению со стандартным CQL алгоритм Adaptive CQL позволяет снизить потери при обучении до 8,4% в низкоразмерном пространстве действий (K=3) и повысить производительность на задачах вне распределения до 118,4%. При этом оптимальная конфигурация Alg1_ACQL (K=10) достигла нормированной производительности 0,8546 при zero-shot переносе. Экспериментально также установлено, что при чрезмерно высокой размерности пространства действий (K=16) адаптивный механизм проявляет тенденцию к вырождению, что указывает на существование оптимальной размерности действий. Результаты исследования предоставляют интерпретируемое, пригодное для повторного использования и робастное интеллектуальное решение для дорогостоящей оптимизации чёрного ящика.
